content: The Muscatine Heart Study in the United States, the Young Finns Study in Finland, and the Northern Finland Birth Cohort of 1966 are examples of longitudinal studies that have examined the relationship between early-life anthropometric measures and later-life health outcomes. Similarly, the 1946 British Birth Cohort and the 1958 British Birth Cohort have provided valuable insights into the long-term effects of childhood growth patterns on adult health. The Western Australian Pregnancy Cohort (Raine) and the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) have also contributed to understanding these associations. The Terneuzen Birth Cohort in the Netherlands and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Growth and Health Study (NGHS) in the United States have explored the impact of childhood and adolescent body mass index (BMI) on adult cardiovascular health. The Longitudinal Study of Juvenile Hypertension in Lithuania and the NHLBI Lipid Research Clinics (LRC) Princeton Prevalence and Follow-Up Study in the United States have further investigated the relationship between early-life weight status and later-life cardiovascular risk. The Child and Adolescent Trial for Cardiovascular Health (CATCH) study in the United States and the East Boston Blood Pressure Study have examined the role of childhood weight and blood pressure in predicting adult cardiovascular outcomes. The Newcastle Thousand Families Cohort Study in the United Kingdom and the Minneapolis Children’s Blood Pressure Study in the United States have also contributed to this body of research. The Old Helsinki Birth Cohort (1924–1933) in Finland and the Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study in New Zealand have provided evidence linking childhood BMI to adult cardiovascular disease and mortality. The National Longitudinal Study of Youth in the United States and the Stockholm Weight Development Study in Sweden have explored similar associations. The German Birth Cohort (LISAplus and GINIplus) and the Fels Longitudinal Study in the United States have examined the tracking of BMI from childhood to adulthood. The Hertfordshire Cohort Study in the United Kingdom and the Group Health Initiative (GHC) of Puget Sound in the United States have also investigated the long-term health effects of early-life weight status. In lowand middle-income countries, studies such as the New Delhi Birth Cohort in India, the Pelotas Birth Cohort of 1993 in Brazil, and the Cebu Longitudinal Health and Nutrition Survey in the Philippines have examined the relationship between childhood growth patterns and adult health outcomes. The Birth to Twenty Cohort in South Africa and the Institute of Nutrition of Central America and Panama Nutritional Trial in Guatemala have also contributed to this research. The Hong Kong Children of 1997 Birth Cohort in China, the Vulnerable Windows Cohort in Jamaica, and the Peruvian Birth Cohort in Peru have explored the impact of early-life growth on adult health. The Pune Children’s Study in India has provided additional evidence on this topic. Quality assessment of the included studies was conducted using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, which evaluates selection, comparability, and outcome measures. Most studies scored highly for the selection of sample populations, with variability in comparability and outcome measures. The studies demonstrated significant heterogeneity in terms of study design, follow-up duration, geographic location, sample size, and definitions of exposure and outcomes. Despite this, the main finding was a consistent association between early-life anthropometric measures and later-life health outcomes, including obesity, cardiovascular disease, and mortality. Fifty-two studies, including 36 cohort or longitudinal studies with over 212,000 individuals, examined the association between childhood and adolescent anthropometric measures and the risk of obesity in later life. These studies highlighted the importance of BMI tracking and the predictive value of early-life weight status for adult obesity. Thirteen studies found that high childhood or adolescent BMI was associated with an increased risk of overweight or obesity in adulthood. Rapid weight gain during infancy and childhood was also a strong predictor of later obesity. Similar trends were observed for height status. Several studies examined the relationship between childhood BMI and cardiovascular disease, including coronary heart disease (CHD), ischemic heart disease, and stroke. Some studies found that lower childhood BMI was associated with increased CHD risk, while others reported a positive association between high childhood BMI and adult cardiovascular events. Carotid artery intima-media thickness (cIMT), a marker of subclinical atherosclerosis, was studied in relation to childhood BMI. Some studies found a positive association, while others reported that the relationship was attenuated after adjusting for adult BMI or waist circumference. Overall, the evidence suggests that early-life anthropometric measures, particularly BMI, are important predictors of adult health outcomes, including obesity, cardiovascular disease, and mortality. These findings underscore the importance of early interventions to promote healthy growth and prevent long-term health risks.
